title: CHAPTER THIRTY-FIVE. On the governance of human beings
latin: CAPUT TRICESIMUM QUINTUM, De gubernatione Hominum. HAec de gubernatione angelorum: sequitur gubernatio hominum, qua Deus eos gubernat et spiritualiter et corporaliter. Hanc regni Dei gubernationis partem in Theologia praecipue consideramus, quia ad subiecti Theologici distinctiorem cognitionem propius facit. Angelorum tamen gubernatio non prorsus insuper habenda fuit, quia et haec illustrat illam. Gubernat autem homines Deus et spiritualiter et corporaliter, quia ex utraque natura sunt mixti. Et hinc Chrysostomus homil. 83 in Matthaeum: Si, inquit, incorporeus esses, nuda incorporea dona tradidisset tibi Deus. Quoniam vero corpori coniuncta est anima tua, in sensibilibus intelligenda tibi traduntur.
english: CHAPTER THIRTY-FIVE. On the governance of human beings.

Thus far concerning the governance of angels: next follows the governance of human beings, by which God governs them both spiritually and bodily. This part of the governance of Gods kingdom we chiefly consider in Theology, because it brings us nearer to a more distinct knowledge of the theological subject. Yet the governance of angels was not to be wholly set aside, because it also illustrates that of humans. God governs human beings both spiritually and bodily, because they are mixed of both natures. Hence Chrysostom (Homily 83 on Matthew): If you were incorporeal, God would have handed you naked incorporeal gifts. But since your soul is joined to a body, things to be understood are handed to you in sensible things.

title: II. Governance before and after the fall; paradise charge and the fall by serpent and free choice
latin: II. Estque primo alia ante lapsum, alia post lapsum. Nam homo ita exornatus a creatore Deo, ut supra demonstratum est, in hortum Edenis, quem paradisum dicimus, collocatus est, ut ibi suavissima contemplatione frueretur, genus suum propagaret, beatam denique vitam, absque omni molestia, morbis et morte, tum singulari Dei providentia, tum beneficio arboris vivificae, ageret, e qua ad beatissimam transferretur. Nimirum Deus, summum bonum, fons ille amoris inexhaustus, primum hominem excellentissimis dotibus ornaverat, eumque tantopere in deliciis habebat, ut in illius intellectu, voluntate, caeterisque potentiis viveret, ambularet, habitaret, operaretur, uniceque vellet ab ipso redamari ex toto corde, mente, viribus. Idcirco, cum universam legem supremus nomothetes homini impressisset, iniunxit quoque ei leviusculum mandatum, pro iure suo quod ut creator in eum habebat, et ut obedientiam eius tentaret, de re quidem per se indifferente, i.e. nec bona nec mala (Gen. 2:16). Satanas vero invidia et odio in Deum omnesque Deo obsequentes creaturas flagrante impulsus, nobilissimum hoc creatoris opificium pessundare conabatur. Quapropter serpentis specie contectus ad feminam, tanquam imperfectiorem et dolis magis patentem, accedit, verba mandatumque Dei corrumpit et calumniose interpretatur. Homines debuissent quidem verbo Dei inhaerere, dolos serpentis declinare: et sane hoc potuissent, siquidem donis quibus pollebant uti voluissent; quin etiam, ut Paulus testatur (1 Tim. 2:14), Adam deceptus non est. Quapropter scientes volentes mandatum Dei posthabuerunt, Diabolo obediverunt, seque in exitium praecipitarunt.
english: II. And first it is one thing before the fall, another after the fall. For the human being, so adorned by God the creator as shown above, was placed in the garden of Eden, which we call paradise, that there he might enjoy most sweet contemplation, propagate his race, and lead a blessed life without all trouble, diseases, and death — both by Gods singular providence and by the benefit of the life-giving tree — from which he would be transferred to the most blessed life. Truly God, the highest good, that inexhaustible fountain of love, had adorned the first human with most excellent gifts, and so delighted in him that He lived, walked, dwelt, and worked in his intellect, will, and other powers, and uniquely willed to be loved again by him from the whole heart, mind, and strength.

Therefore, when the supreme Lawgiver had impressed the universal law on the human, He also enjoined a lighter command, by His right as creator and to test obedience, concerning a thing in itself indifferent — neither good nor evil (Genesis 2:16). But Satan, driven by burning envy and hatred against God and all creatures obedient to God, tried to overthrow this noblest work of the creator. Therefore, covered in a serpents form, he approaches the woman as the weaker and more open to deceit, corrupts Gods words and command, and interprets them slanderously. Humans ought indeed to have clung to Gods word and declined the serpents snares; and they could have, had they been willing to use the gifts they possessed; indeed, as Paul witnesses (1 Timothy 2:14), Adam was not deceived. Therefore knowingly and willingly they set Gods command aside, obeyed the Devil, and cast themselves into ruin.

title: III–V. Modes of governing humans: instinct, institution, and teaching
latin: III. Secundo alia est per modum instinctus, alia per modum institutionis, alia per modum impletionis. IV. Per modum institutionis Deus homines gubernat docendo. V. Sic insigniore respectu tum immediate tum mediate Deus homines docet. Immediate, cum per se ipsum, per Filium et Spiritum Sanctum, per angelos, per verbum revelatum, per legem naturae impressam, per conscientiam, per somnia et visiones, per miracula et prodigia, per inspirationem specialem. Mediate, cum per parentes, magistros, ministros verbi, magistratus, et alios homines, quibus verbum suum commendat. Mediate vocatis cum hac adiunctione est obtemperandum, si nihil principiis addant, demant aut contrarium doceant (1 Thess. 5:21; 1 Ioh. 4:1).
english: III. Second, governance is one thing by way of instinct, another by way of institution, another by way of fulfillment. IV. By way of institution God governs human beings by teaching. V. Thus in a more notable respect God teaches humans both immediately and mediately. Immediately, when by Himself, by the Son and Holy Spirit, by angels, by revealed word, by the law of nature impressed, by conscience, by dreams and visions, by miracles and wonders, by special inspiration. Mediately, when through parents, teachers, ministers of the word, magistrates, and other humans to whom He commits His word. Those mediately called are to be obeyed with this proviso: if they add nothing to the principles, take nothing away, or teach nothing contrary (1 Thessalonians 5:21; 1 John 4:1).

title: VIII–XI. Bodily means; covenants of marriage and natural religion
latin: VIII. Per res corporeas aut naturales Deus etiam homines gubernat, tum ad conservationem vitae, tum ad disciplinam et poenam, tum ad beneficia et monita. XI. Porro cum insigniore respectu Deus homines docendo gubernat, quando foedera inter ipsos, et inter se ac illos constituit, secundum ea agit. Deus inter homines constituit foedus coniugii, de quo supra vidimus cum doceremus de creatione hominis (Gen. 1:28-29; 2:24; Mal. 2:14), quod foedus coniuges inter se fide castitatis servare et operarum utilium concordi societate firmare debent. Inter se vero et homines Deus in principio constituit solenne foedus religionis naturalis (Gen. 1:28-30; 2:16-17; 3:1-4, 22). Et hic homines decuerat fides circumspecta et obedientia specialis erga illam legem, cum hac confessione iure ipsos puniri si peccarent, uti et se ad omne obsequium obligatos intelligebant (Gen. 3:3). Et secundum hoc foedus Deus sic egit, ut homines suae libertati permiserit, ut ex eventu liquet. Hi vero suapte culpa, deceptore Diabolo, in peccatum lapsi sunt, et propterea iuste a Deo affliguntur (Gen. 3; 2 Cor. 11:3). Unde et sobolem genuerunt ad similitudinem suam (Gen. 5:3; Iob 15:14-16; Psal. 51:7; Rom. 5:12).
english: VIII. Through bodily or natural things God also governs human beings — for conserving life, for discipline and punishment, and for benefits and warnings. XI. Further, in a more notable respect God governs humans by teaching when He constitutes covenants among them, and between Himself and them, and acts according to those covenants.

God constituted among humans the covenant of marriage, of which we saw above when teaching the creation of humankind (Genesis 1:28-29; 2:24; Malachi 2:14), which spouses ought to keep between themselves by the faith of chastity and to strengthen by a concordant partnership of useful works. And between Himself and humans God at the beginning constituted the solemn covenant of natural religion (Genesis 1:28-30; 2:16-17; 3:1-4, 22). Here circumspect faith and special obedience toward that law became humans, with this confession that they were justly punished if they sinned, as they also understood themselves obliged to every obedience (Genesis 3:3).

And according to this covenant God so acted that He permitted humans their liberty, as the event makes clear. But they by their own fault, the Devil deceiving, fell into sin, and therefore are justly afflicted by God (Genesis 3; 2 Corinthians 11:3). Hence also they begot offspring after their own likeness (Genesis 5:3; Job 15:14-16; Psalm 51:7; Romans 5:12).

title: XII. Governance by fulfillment: permitting, impeding, effecting, tolerating; Cap. 35 close
latin: XII. Per modum impletionis Deus gubernat homines, cum aliquid spirituale vel corporale permittit aut impedit, aut efficit eis benefaciens vel eos affligens, aut in eis tolerat. Hos modos implendi videbis 2 Petr. 2:4 et seqq. Verum enimvero lapsione primorum parentum salutares modi docendi sunt enervati, et modi implendi impediti, ut ex sequenti cap. 37 patebit.
english: XII. By way of fulfillment God governs human beings when He permits or impedes something spiritual or bodily, or effects it while benefiting or afflicting them, or tolerates it in them. You will see these modes of fulfillment in 2 Peter 2:4 and following. But in truth, by the fall of the first parents the salutary modes of teaching were weakened, and the modes of fulfillment impeded, as will appear from the following chapter 37.
